κλαγγ-ή , ἡ, metapl. dat.
A. “κλαγγί”
Ibyc. 56
: (κλάζω):—any sharp sound, e.g. twang of the bow, Il. 1.49 ; scream of birds, esp. cranes, to which are compared confused cries of a throng, 3.3 , Od. 11.605 , cf. Il. 2.100 , 10.523 ; grunting of swine, Od. 14.412 ; later, howling of wolves and lions, h.Hom. 14.4 , cf. 27.8 ; hissing of serpents, Pi. Dith. 2.18 (pl.), A. Th. 381 (pl.); baying of dogs, X. Cyn. 4.5 , etc.; also, of musical instruments, Telest. 4 , Mnesim. 4.57 (anap.); of song, S. Tr. 208 (lyr.); κ. ἀηδόνειος (leg. -όνιος) Nicom. Trag. 1 ; κ. δύσφατος, of Cassandra's prophecies, A. Ag. 1152 (lyr.); of the scream of the Harpies, A.R. 2.269 .
From A Greek-English Lexicon (Henry George Liddell, Robert Scott, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1940)
